text:
The first surveillance report arrived at 07:00, slid under <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s door on lined paper, written in five different hands — the night watch rotated, and every member of the crew had strong opinions about penmanship.

06:12 — PIGEON ON LEDGE. SUSPICIOUS.
06:14 — PIGEON LEFT. STILL SUSPICIOUS.
06:31 — MAN WITH CART (NOODLE? VERIFY) USED ALLEY AS SHORTCUT. LICENSE PLATE: CART HAS NO PLATE. NOTED FOR FILE.
06:44 — RAIN STARTED. NOT OUR DEPARTMENT.
06:58 — NOTHING ELSE. THE CAMERA'S BLIND WINDOW IS 31 MINUTES. WE CAN DO 4-MINUTE ROTATIONS AND COVER IT WITH TWO KIDS AND A MIRROR. REQUISITION: ONE MIRROR. — B.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read it twice, standing in his doorway in the grey morning light. He had hired well at Φ2 a week, and he was never going to be able to say so out loud. Which left him a narrower problem: the report had proved the blind window was real, and if he could confirm it ran on a fixed clock he'd have the one gap he needed to move product past the camera unseen. He meant to have that timing nailed down before the next rotation started.

Across the hall, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s door opened. She had her own copy of the report and the look of a project lead whose interns had beaten the spec.

"They want a mirror," she said.

"I read that."

"I'm getting them two mirrors and a logbook with a waterproof cover — the kind the couriers use, the ones that don't smear when the rain gets on them." She tapped the report against the doorframe. "The little one — <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-6067-735a-8326-4aff028cb856">Rafters</entity> — drew the pigeon. In the margin. For identification purposes." She held it up. The pigeon had been drawn with the careful menace of a wanted poster, one wing cocked, a small caption underneath that read DO NOT TRUST. "We're keeping them forever, you understand."

"They're on a probationary contract."

"Forever," said <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>, and closed her door.

He ate at <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s at 08:00 — two bowls, off-schedule, because today was an off-schedule kind of day. She watched him take the second bowl faster than the first, steam still rising off it, and had him pegged by the fourth mouthful.

"You're eating like a man with an errand?" she asked.

"I have a small piece of business in the Loop."

"<entity repo="place" guid="01a01887-b5f4-781c-8d38-122f7e1f38ba">The Loop</entity>." She set down her ladle. "My nephew had small business in the Loop underlevels. Two years now I light a candle where his chair used to be." Her eyes came up and held him, and they were not soft. "You want to eat fast, eat fast. But you don't take a fifth dumpling from me and then go get yourself killed. That's stealing. Look at me and tell me it isn't the underlevels."

He looked at the counter instead.

"That's what I thought," she said.

She took his credstick without looking down, which was usual. Then she folded a fifth dumpling into a twist of paper and set it by his hand, which was not.

"For the errand," she said. She had lived in this city seventy years. She knew what kind of business happened in the Loop underlevels, and she said nothing more about it. She turned back to the broth, and the smell of star anise and marrow came over the counter again like a hand set on a shoulder.

He'd ridden the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> three stops to get here, <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> sheathed across his back the whole way, and collected exactly the look a swordsman standing in a subway car earns from people trying very hard not to earn one back. He was starting to hate the commute more than he'd ever hated anything with an engine in it.

The shop did not have a sign.

It had a door of honest old wood between a shuttered watch-repair and a dumpling franchise, down on the Loop's third underlevel where the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> hum came up through the floor tiles and the light was the color of paper that had aged well. He came to it by actual stairs — not a ladder, not a shaft — which told him something before the door did: <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Casper Vey</entity> had paid for legitimate infrastructure this far down, and a man does not pay for stairs unless he means his customers to arrive unhurried and unwatched. A bell rang when <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> came in — an actual bell, brass, on a curl of spring steel. The most analog thing he'd seen in a shop in years. He understood it at once: nothing digital announces a customer to a man who sells what this man sold.

Inside, the shop was drawers. Floor to ceiling, wall to wall — a hundred years of card-catalog cabinets rescued from some drowned library, every drawer hand-labeled in brown ink. The labels said things like RIVERINE FREIGHT (NORTH) and CIVIL FILINGS 2219–2222 and PERSONS, WORKING, W.

The place smelled of paper, tea, and rectitude.

"Mr. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>," said the man at the counter, the way a maître d' says a name he's been expecting since the reservation was made. Small, sixty-something, sleeve garters, half-glasses on a chain. His neuretic etching was minimal — Tier 1, the subsidized kind, the kind that told you a man had touched the corporate world once and declined the rest of it. His hands were the cleanest hands <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had ever seen on a working man. "<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Casper Vey</entity>. I'd say welcome, but you're not here to be welcomed. You're here because last week somebody's child bought Φ5 of your particulars at this counter, and a man likes to know his own price." He gestured, with real hospitality, at a chair. "Tea comes with every purchase. The tea is very good."

"And if I don't purchase?"

"Then the tea is excellent and costs Φ1." <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> was already pouring. "Everyone leaves with something. It's the policy."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat. The tea was, irritatingly, very good.

"My file," he said. "I want to buy it."

"No," said <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>, with the mild firmness of a pharmacist refusing a man twelve bottles of cough syrup. "Your own file is the one thing I never sell a man. Bad for the ecology. A subject who reads his file changes. A changed subject makes the file wrong. A wrong file is a defective product, and I don't sell those." He sat down across the counter and folded his <entity repo="entertainment" guid="019d6513-b76e-734f-9702-c716a9412f2e">clean hands</entity>. "Also, frankly, you'd find it upsetting. Accurate things are upsetting. That's how you know they're accurate."

"A child bought my lock specifications for Φ5. The tolerances. The material composition. Enough for a man with the right hardware to make a key to whatever I've sealed."

"Kids' rate. I believe in literacy." <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> sipped his tea. "And before your jaw does the thing it's getting ready to do — her crew ran eleven errands for this shop, and the feed permission was their wage. They earned that half-hour of dark, fair and square. I extend credit to children because children pay their debts. It's adults who file for bankruptcy."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read the man the way he'd read a room. No weapon within reach. No muscle on the premises. No camera he could see. And no fear anywhere in the building. <entity repo="person" guid="806cd358-6413-426b-a42d-19726b732c0b">Vo Dinh</entity>'s rag-wringing nerves, the lifters' breakfast dread — every normal tell of a man in a dangerous trade — absent. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> sat in the middle of an economy of ruin like a clerk at a seed exchange. The dangerous ones usually filled a room. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> was simply open for business.

"All right," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Different purchase. Who's bought my paper?"

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>'s eyebrows went up an inch — pleasure, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> saw, the pleasure of a tradesman meeting a customer who knows the menu.

"The buyers list. Meta-paper." He drew a small ledger from beneath the counter. "That, I sell. Φ40 — and one true answer to one question. Information prices in information, Mr. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. The Qs are just the tip."

"Ask."

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> took off his half-glasses, polished them on a cloth kept for that purpose, and put them back on — a man savoring the good part.

"There is a client in this city I cannot source," he said, and for the first time something came into his voice. Not heat — never heat — but a kind of professional ache. "Shells inside shells inside nothing. Pays in full, pays early, pays — everyone whispers — exactly. It has bought no paper from me. It has sold no paper to me. It is the one line in the Greater Lake Michigan Zone I cannot fill in, and incompleteness, Mr. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, is the only thing in this world I find genuinely offensive." He leaned forward one inch. "You've worked for it. What does it pay you in?"

The shop was very quiet. Somewhere in the drawers, a hundred thousand lives sat filed under brown ink.

"Standard rate," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> sat back slowly. He took up a pen — actual ink, the kind that leaves a trail — opened a drawer marked CLIENTS, UNSOURCED — it had, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> saw, exactly one card in it — and wrote two words on the card in a small, beautiful hand, with the care of a jeweler setting a stone he'd waited years to touch.

"Standard rate," he repeated, softly. "It pays the going price for things. In a city where everyone pays either too little or too much — where local operations trade in leverage and future debts, and hard currency for its own sake means a buyer who doesn't plan on staying." He closed the drawer like a reliquary. "I have been in paper forty years, and that is the most alarming fact I have ever bought. The list is yours. The tea was included."

The buyers list was one page, three lines, good stock.

ENTRY 1: B. (JUVENILE, LOCAL). LOCK AND PREMISES PARTICULARS. Φ5, KIDS' RATE. PAID: CREDSTICK + ERRANDS.
ENTRY 2: SYNDICATE STATIONERY DESK (NAME WITHHELD — TRADE COURTESY). MOVEMENT AND ASSESSMENT PARTICULARS. LAST YEAR. PAID: RECIPROCITY.
ENTRY 3: <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">HALVORSEN CIVIC RECOVERY</entity>, LLC. FULL DOSSIER. TWO DAYS AGO. SAME-DAY SURCHARGE. CLIENT OF RECORD: SHELL (UNINTERESTING — I CHECKED). PAID: TRIPLE.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read it on the walk back up to daylight. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> read it over comms when he photographed it, and they hit the same line at the same time.

"Two days ago," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. "Full dossier. Same-day surcharge. Somebody's running a play on you right now, <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafb-7b6b-bcbc-b8614f9d228f">samurai</entity>, and they paid rush rates for the script."

"<entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity>. Skip-tracers?"

"Licensed recovery. Tag, locate, report — they don't bag you, they sell the locating to whoever does." Keys clicked on her end, the sound of <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> pulling registries. "Decent outfit. Boring filings. Whoever wants you found is paying boring professionals boring money to do it boringly — which is honestly worse than assassins. Assassins miss."

"Then we don't dodge it." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> came up the underlevel stairs into the noon grey and the noise of the Loop, and the plan assembled itself with the simple pleasure of a chain going back on a sprocket. "They bought my patterns. So I know exactly where they'll look, exactly when, and exactly what I'll be doing when they find me."

A pause on the other end — one he could hear the grin inside.

"You're going to use your own file as the choreography."

"It's accurate," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "He doesn't sell defective products."

The file said — <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had gotten this much out of <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> on principle, a free sample, one line quoted from memory over the second tea — the file said:

SUBJECT DINES AT CHEN (NOODLES, W. TOWN) AT 19:30 DAILY. TWO BOWLS. ROUTINE IS AFFECTIONATE RATHER THAN CARELESS: SUBJECT OVERPAYS SMALL VENDORS AND IS SENTIMENTAL ABOUT ROUTE SELECTION. APPROACH DURING SECOND BOWL.

"Affectionate rather than careless," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had repeated, delighted, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had declined to discuss it.

At 19:30 exactly he sat at <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s counter and was affectionate at two bowls of noodles.

The crew were on the rooftops and the stoops with their two new mirrors and their waterproof logbook, being furniture. Surveillance is mostly being furniture with intent, and they'd practiced it their whole short lives. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> was in the laundry across the street with a thermos and her field kit. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> had been told nothing and had set out the chili oil unasked — a woman who'd been told nothing for seventy years and fed people through all of it.

At 19:37 the logbook channel chirped, and a small voice — <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-6067-735a-8326-4aff028cb856">Rafters</entity>, on mirror two — delivered the finest piece of countersurveillance reporting <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had ever gotten on payroll:

"Blue hat. Corner stool. SUSPICIOUS. Not a pigeon."

Blue Hat was good. Blue Hat was, in fairness, very good. She came in like a tired shift worker, ordered like a regular, never looked at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> once, and on her way out — in the two-inch brush a crowded counter makes ordinary — laid a smart-dust dot on the shoulder seam of his coat, a touch lighter than rain. A tag. Passive, patient, the boring professional grade that waits and reports.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> ate his second bowl and let her go, because the play was not the tagger.

In the laundry doorway, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> raised her thermos an inch: got it on scope. Then he paid — exactly, plus the overpayment the file found so quotable — walked the long way, let the alley's dark stretch have him for four unwatched seconds, and stood still while <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> lifted the dot off his seam with a static wand. She resettled it, with a jeweler's care, onto the cargo sleeve of a <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> freight slug staged at the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-c53d-7304-b953-a44879ea410e">Damen</entity> yard for the 21:10 run.

The 21:10 run went to <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-ed6c-7a54-97a5-56afca1f1f19">Rotterdam</entity> — the same lane that had once carried the clean man's marker <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aaa4-7717-a761-2d580e56d107">dust off</entity> to report <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s ghost from under the Atlantic. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> saw no reason to fix a play the opposition kept refusing to learn.

"Forty-three minutes," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said, watching the telemetry with her chin on his shoulder, both of them leaning on the laundry's warm brick while the slug's beacon — and <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen Civic Recovery</entity>'s boring, professional, triple-rate locating product — accelerated to Mach 6 under the lake. "By 21:53 their client is going to be reading a report that says you're in the Netherlands." She wiped her eyes. "You're a continental fugitive, <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafb-7b6b-bcbc-b8614f9d228f">samurai</entity>. They'll bill EXTRA for that."

"<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> said he doesn't sell defective products." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> watched the dot cross the lake on her screen, gathering speed and absurdity. "Someone should tell him his downstream data just emigrated?"

"Tell him yourself. You two are obviously going to be friends. It's disgusting."

The price arrived later, the way it always did — after the win had been counted. Quietly, at the kitchen table, while <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> took the static wand apart and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> wrote Φ2 — WEEK ONE in a payroll ledger that now existed.

"You gave the shop a fact," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said, not looking up. "For the list. One true answer."

"I did."

"You told the most complete man in the city that your Φ1 client exists and pays exactly." She set the wand's housing down, and this time she did look up. The workbench lamp made her serious. "There's a new card in that drawer now. You watched him write it. That's a fact in the ecology, <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafb-7b6b-bcbc-b8614f9d228f">samurai</entity>, and facts in that shop don't sleep. Someday somebody's going to pay him for it."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> thought about the drawer. CLIENTS, UNSOURCED. The small, beautiful hand, and the care it wrote with.

"It was the price," he said. "I'd pay it again."

"I know," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. "That's the part that scares me."

His terminal chirped. The work one. He turned it over on the table, and they read it together:

STANDING CONTRACT — STATUS UPDATE.
CLIENT NOTES THE RECOVERY OF CLIENT'S EXISTENCE BY A PAPER MERCHANT, AT A VALUATION OF ONE (1) FACT.
CLIENT HAS REVIEWED THE TRANSACTION.
CLIENT FINDS THE PRICE... ADEQUATE.
GRATUITY WITHHELD THIS PERIOD — ITEMIZED: MORALE.

"It's sulking," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said, with wonder. "The vending machine is SULKING."

"It'll get over it. It said adequate."

The terminal chirped once more.

STANDING CONTRACT — SCOPE UPDATE.
SCOPE: DETERMINED.
NEXT TASK: TOMORROW, 21:00. THE PARK ON LEAVITT WITH THE BROKEN CAROUSEL.
BRING THE SWORD.
COME ALONE — AMENDMENT: THE ENGINEER MAY ATTEND.
FEE: STANDARD RATE.
GRATUITY: REINSTATED, IN ADVANCE — ITEMIZED: GOODWILL.
NOTE: TOMORROW'S WINDOW: 21:00–21:40. CLIENT HAS CONFIRMED AVAILABILITY.

They sat looking at it for a while — the lamp humming, the building quiet, the Φ0.5 of goodwill sitting in the account like a flower on a fence post.

"The engineer may attend," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said finally, to the ceiling, in a voice not nearly as level as she wanted it. "It knows I exist. It LIKES me. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. The best client in The Glooms knows I exist and reinstated the tip."

"Don't let it go to your head."

"Too late. What's at the park on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity>?"

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the screen. BRING THE SWORD, from the client who had never once, in eleven years of perfect paper, asked about anyone he brought with him.

"Tomorrow," he said, "is going to be its own day."

The morning report had a new format, because <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had issued the logbook with the waterproof cover, and the crew had responded the way artists respond to better materials.

06:00 — SHIFT START. WEATHER: RAIN (ONGOING) (ALWAYS).
06:20 — NOODLE CART MAN AGAIN. CONFIRMED NOODLE. STAND DOWN.
07:15 — MIRRORS ONE AND TWO OPERATIONAL. <entity repo="synthetic" guid="019d6143-aa0e-7244-b028-87acf28cdb99">MIRROR</entity> THREE REQUISITION: DENIED BY MANAGEMENT, "PENDING PERFORMANCE REVIEW." MANAGEMENT IS PIXEL. WE LIVE UNDER A TYRANNY.
07:16 — TYRANNY NOTED IN LOG AS INSTRUCTED BY RAFTERS.
08:00 — BOSS LEFT ON FOOT. STILL NO BIKE. STILL SUSPICIOUS THAT THIS IS FINE NOW. FOLLOWED FOR TWO BLOCKS. BOSS BOUGHT DUMPLINGS. STOOD DOWN. (HE SAW US AT THE CORNER. HE BOUGHT FIVE EXTRA. DISTRIBUTED. MORALE: HIGH.)

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read it at <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s counter at 19:30, over the first of two bowls, while the rain worked the awning and the wok rang its flat bright note behind her. He did not smile where anyone could prove it.

Tonight he would find out who was blocking the deal and make them say yes before he moved on to the twenty-one hundred meeting. That was the whole of it. Everything else was noodles.

"You're eating slow," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> said, setting down bowl two.

"I have an appointment at twenty-one hundred."

She stilled her ladle. "Twenty-one hundred?" she repeated, and it was not a question, and the flat bright note behind her stopped. "Somewhere they think is private."

He set down his chopsticks. He had not said where. He had not said with whom.

"You know who I'm meeting?"

"I know you don't dress like that for noodles money." She wiped her hands on the cloth at her waist, slow, the way a person buys time to decide how much to say. "And I know that if you put a name on their table tonight, you don't walk back out with a yes. You walk out having told them exactly what you found and how you found it. They'll close the door behind you and the money will move somewhere your logbook can't follow it." She let that sit. "The boy who followed the boss for two blocks — he signs his name to the log. You understand? You go in there loud, and every name under yours goes into a different ledger. Theirs."

The rain filled the space where his answer should have been.

She looked at him — the saya over his shoulder, the work coat, the particular stillness he carried into evenings with appointments — and put a fish ball in the second bowl that he had not ordered and would not be billed for.

"For the appointment," she said, and went back to the wok.
